title: Highest-Protein Meats: Ranking per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Meats per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare cooked rabbit, chicken, turkey, beef, lamb and pork by protein per 100 grams and realistic serving.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked lean meats by protein content.

excerpt: Cooked rabbit and chicken breast are among the most protein-dense lean meats, while turkey, beef, lamb and lean pork are close behind, generally around 27–30 g per 100 g.
content_html:
Most lean cooked meats fall within a fairly narrow range of protein: roughly 27–33 g per 100 g. Cut, fat content and water loss during cooking can change the number as much as the animal species.

Lean cooked meat ranking

MeatProtein/100 g
Cooked rabbit~33 g
Skinless chicken breast31 g
Skinless turkey breast29.5 g
Lean beef~29 g
Lean lamb~28 g
Lean pork~27 g

Rabbit and chicken

Cooked rabbit can reach about 33 g protein/100 g and chicken breast about 31 g. In a 5-ounce / 142 g serving, that is roughly 47 g versus 44 g.

Turkey and beef

Turkey breast and lean beef are both near 29–30 g/100 g. Beef's bigger nutritional difference is iron: lean beef often provides roughly 2–3 mg/100 g compared with about 1 mg in turkey breast.

Pork

Lean pork loin or tenderloin is around 27 g/100 g, close to turkey and beef. Bacon, by contrast, can exceed 40–50 g fat/100 g while tenderloin may be near 5 g, showing why the cut matters more than the word “pork.”

Why cooked meat looks higher in protein

Raw chicken breast may be around 22–23 g protein/100 g, compared with about 31 g after cooking. Water loss concentrates the protein.

If 120 g raw meat containing 27 g protein finishes at 90 g after cooking, those 27 g are now spread across less weight.

Cured and dried meats

Jerky and cured ham can exceed fresh cooked meat in protein per 100 g because much of their water has been removed. They also concentrate sodium. Jerky may exceed 30 g protein/100 g while carrying hundreds of milligrams or more of sodium per serving, so it is not nutritionally equivalent to a fresh steak.

Protein by serving

Meat5 oz / 142 g cooked
Rabbit~47 g protein
Chicken44 g
Turkey42 g
Lean beef~41 g
Lean pork~38 g

What else matters

Fat varies enormously by cut; red meat generally provides more iron; fresh unsalted meat is low in sodium while many processed meats are high. Sausage, deli meat and a fresh loin are not interchangeable simply because they come from the same animal.

Bottom line

Rabbit and chicken breast are near the top for protein concentration, but turkey, beef, lamb and lean pork are close. Choosing a lean cut and varying protein sources usually matters more than chasing a two-gram difference.

Sources

Composition values come from USDA FoodData Central; cooking-water context comes from USDA FSIS.

faq.question: Which meat has the most protein?
faq.answer: Among lean cooked meats, rabbit can be around 33 g/100 g and chicken breast about 31 g/100 g.

faq.question: Does chicken have more protein than beef?
faq.answer: Chicken breast is about 31 g/100 g and many lean beef cuts around 29 g, so the difference is small.

faq.question: Why does cooked meat show more protein?
faq.answer: Cooking removes water and concentrates protein into less weight.
